attack_technique: Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
description: Adversaries may attempt to cause a denial of service by exhausting the target's connection state tables. A SYN Flood exploits the standard TCP three-way handshake by sending a massive volume of SYN (synchronize) packets to the target but intentionally failing to send the final ACK (acknowledge) packet. This leaves the server with thousands of 'half-open' connections, rapidly exhausting its SYN backlog and preventing legitimate users from establishing new TCP connections.

patterns.description: Specific manipulations of the Transport Control Protocol (TCP) connection initiation process.

features.name: Extreme SYN Flag Ratio
features.description: An abnormally high percentage of incoming packets have only the SYN flag set (High SYN Flag Cnt). The attacker is constantly requesting new connections without ever sending data.

features.name: Missing ACK Completion
features.description: The client completely ignores the server's SYN-ACK responses and never sends the final ACK packet required to establish a fully open, stateful TCP connection.

patterns.description: Anomalies in the flow of packets, indicating a highly asymmetric attack.

features.name: Forward Packet Flood
features.description: A massive surge in packets sent from the client to the server (High Fwd Pkts/s), specifically consisting of lightweight connection requests rather than heavy data payloads.

features.name: Asymmetric Backward Flow
features.description: Because the connections are never completed and data is never requested, the server sends very few backward packets (Low Bwd Pkts/s)—usually just the initial SYN-ACK responses before the connection drops.

patterns.description: Behaviors related to the duration of flows and the exhaustion of server memory.

features.name: Truncated Flow Durations
features.description: Because the TCP handshakes are never completed, network flow trackers will either log exceptionally short, incomplete flows (Low Flow Duration) or record connections that strictly hit the server's SYN timeout limit.

features.name: SYN Backlog Exhaustion
features.description: The attack rapidly fills the operating system's connection queue (SYN backlog), causing the server to silently drop or reject new, legitimate TCP connection requests.

patterns.description: Contextual indicators for distinguishing the attack from legitimate traffic behavior.

features.name: Source IP Spoofing
features.description: SYN floods almost universally utilize highly randomized, spoofed source IP addresses. This prevents the attacker from receiving the SYN-ACKs and makes IP-based blocklists ineffective.

features.name: Peak Traffic Resemblance (False Positive Filtering)
features.description: During legitimate peak traffic events (flash crowds), servers will naturally experience elevated SYN counts. However, in legitimate scenarios, these SYNs are almost immediately followed by ACKs to complete the handshake.
